en: Thus have I heard— Dīgha Nikāya 12, the Lohiccasutta.
On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of about five hundred bhikkhus, he arrived at Sālavatikā.

Now at that time, the brahmin Lohicca was residing at Sālavatikā—a prosperous place, well-supplied with grass, timber, water, and grain, a royal domain granted by King Pasenadi of Kosala as a royal gift and a brahmin’s fief.
At that time, a pernicious view such as this had arisen in the brahmin Lohicca:
“Suppose here a recluse or a brahmin should attain a wholesome state, yet having attained a wholesome state, he does not declare it to another. For what can one person do for another?
Just as if one were to cut an old bond and make another new bond, even so, I say, is this evil state of greed; for what can one person do for another?”
The brahmin Lohicca heard:

"Friends, the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a great community of monks, numbering about five hundred monks, has arrived at Sālavatikā.
Now, such is the excellent reputation that has arisen concerning the venerable Gotama:"

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having personally realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
“It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin Lohicca addressed Rosika the barber:

“Come, my dear Rosika, go to where the ascetic Gotama is; having approached him, inquire in my name after the ascetic Gotama’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical vigor, strength, and well-being, saying:”
“Master Gotama, the brahmin Lohicca inquires after your health, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, strength, and well-being;
and please say this for him:
‘May Master Gotama, together with the community of monks, consent to accept a meal from the brahmin Lohicca tomorrow.’”
“Yes, sir,” the barber Rosika replied to the brahmin Lohicca.
He approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the barber Rosika said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the brahmin Lohicca inquires after the Blessed One’s health, asking whether he is free from illness and affliction, and is light, strong, and dwelling in comfort.
And he says this:
‘Venerable sir, may the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, please accept tomorrow’s meal from the brahmin Lohicca.’”
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then Rosika the barber, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, approached the brahmin Lohicca. Having approached, he said this to the brahmin Lohicca:
“We have indeed spoken to that Blessed One on behalf of your words:
‘Venerable sir, the brahmin Lohicca inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, strength, and well-being;
and he says this:’”
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One, together with the community of bhikkhus, please accept tomorrow’s meal from the brahmin Lohicca.
And the Blessed One consented by silence.
Then, when that night had passed, the brahmin Lohicca had various kinds of fine hard and soft food prepared in his own residence and addressed Rosika the barber:
“Come, friend Rosika, go to where the ascetic Gotama is; having approached him, announce the time to the ascetic Gotama:
‘It is time, sir Gotama, the meal is ready.
“Very well, sir,” Rosika the barber replied to the brahmin Lohicca, and he went to where the Blessed One was. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Rosika the barber announced the time to the Blessed One:
"It is time, Bhante; the meal is ready.
Then, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One approached Sālavatikā together with the community of monks.
Now at that time, Rosika the barber was following closely behind the Blessed One.
Then Rosika the barber said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, such an evil view has arisen in the brahmin Lohicca:..."
‘In this case, a recluse or a brahmin might attain a wholesome state; having attained a wholesome state, he would not declare it to another, thinking:
“What can one person do for another?
It would be just as if, having cut an old bond, one were to make another new bond.”’
"In this way, I say that this evil state of greed is exactly so:
for what can one person do for another?
"It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would detach the brahmin Lohicca from this evil speculative view."
“Perhaps it might be so, Rosika; perhaps it might be so, Rosika.
Then the Blessed One approached the residence of the brahmin Lohicca; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the brahmin Lohicca, with his own hands, served and satisfied the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent hard foods and soft foods.
1. The Inquiry of the Brahmin Lohicca Then the brahmin Lohicca, when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As the brahmin Lohicca was sitting there to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Is it true, Lohicca, that such an evil view has arisen in you:
‘Suppose here a recluse or a brahmin were to attain a wholesome state; having attained a wholesome state, he should not declare it to another, for what can one person do for another?
It would be just as if, having cut an old bond, one were to make another new bond;’”
“I say that this evil state of greed is exactly like that; for what can one person do for another?
“It is so, Master Gotama.
“What do you think, Lohicca?”
“Do you not, however, reside at Sālavatikā?
“Yes, Master Gotama.
“Now, Lohicca, if someone were to say this:”
“The brahmin Lohicca presides over Sālavatikā.
Whatever wealth is produced and accumulated in Sālavatikā, that brahmin Lohicca alone would enjoy it and would not give anything to others.
Does one who speaks thus create an obstacle for those who depend upon him, or not?
“An obstacle-maker, Master Gotama.
“Being an obstacle-maker, does he have compassion for their welfare or lack compassion for their welfare?
“He lacks compassion for their welfare, Master Gotama.”
“Does one who is compassionate toward those who are harmful have a mind established in loving-kindness toward them, or does it have enmity?
“Enmity, Master Gotama.
“When a mind of enmity is established, is there wrong view or right view?”
“Wrong view, Master Gotama.
“For one with wrong view, Lohicca, I declare one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.”
“What do you think, Lohicca,
does not King Pasenadi of Kosala reside over Kāsī and Kosala?
“Yes, Master Gotama.”
“Lohicca, if anyone were to say this:
‘King Pasenadi of Kosala rules over Kāsī and Kosala;
whatever wealth is produced and accumulated in Kāsī and Kosala, King Pasenadi of Kosala alone should enjoy it by himself and should not give any to others’—what do you think?”
“Does one who speaks thus create an obstacle for those who depend upon King Pasenadi of Kosala—both you and others—or not?
“He does create an obstacle, Master Gotama.
“Being one who creates an obstacle, is he sympathetic toward their welfare or unsympathetic toward their welfare?”
“One who is compassionate toward those who are harmful, Master Gotama.
“Does one who is compassionate toward those who are harmful have a mind established in friendliness toward them, or does it have enmity?
“It has enmity, Master Gotama.”
“When a mind of enmity is present, is there wrong view or right view?
“Wrong view, Master Gotama.
“For one with wrong view, Lohicca, I declare one of two destinations: [either this world or the next].”
"Either hell or the animal realm.
Thus, Lohicca, it would be as if someone were to say:
'The brahmin Lohicca dwells at Sālavatikā;'"
‘Whatever income and production there is from Sālavatikā, let the brahmin Lohicca alone enjoy it; he should not give anything to others.
One who speaks thus becomes an obstacle-maker for those who depend on him.
Being an obstacle-maker, he is one who does not wish them well. To one who does not wish them well, a hostile mind is established. When a hostile mind is established, there is wrong view.
"In the same way, Lohicca, suppose someone were to say this:
'Here, a recluse or a brahmin might attain a wholesome state; having attained a wholesome state, he would not declare it to another, for what can one person do for another?
It is just as if, having cut an old bond, one were to make another new bond... [and so on].
‘He will do it. Speaking thus, he [disparages] those sons of good family who, having approached the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata,
attain such a sublime distinction, and realize the fruit of stream-entry, and realize the fruit of once-returning.
They realize the fruit of non-returning; they realize arhatship;
and for those who are ripening these divine wombs for the production of divine existences, he becomes an obstacle. Being an obstacle, he is one who lacks compassion for their welfare.
In one who lacks compassion for their welfare, a hostile mind is established. When a hostile mind is established, wrong view arises.
"Lohicca, for one of wrong view, I declare one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.
Thus, Lohicca, if anyone were to say this:"
“King Pasenadi of Kosala rules over Kāsī and Kosala.
Whatever wealth is produced and accumulated in Kāsī and Kosala, King Pasenadi of Kosala alone should enjoy it by himself and should not give it to others.
By speaking thus, he creates an obstacle for those who depend on King Pasenadi of Kosala—both you and others.
Being an obstacle-maker, one is compassionate toward what is harmful; for one who is compassionate toward what is harmful, a hostile mind is established;
when a hostile mind is established, there is wrong view. In the same way, Lohicca, if someone were to say this:
“Suppose here a recluse or a brahmin should attain a wholesome state; having attained a wholesome state, he should not declare it to another. For what can one person do for another?”
"Just as if... what indeed can one person do for another?
Speaking thus, he [rejects] those sons of good family who, having approached the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, [attain] such a sublime...
They attain distinction; they realize the fruit of stream-entry, they realize the fruit of once-returning, they realize the fruit of non-returning, and they realize arhatship as well.
Furthermore, it acts as an obstacle to those celestial wombs that bring about rebirth in divine existences.

Being one who creates obstacles, he is compassionate toward what is harmful; for one who is compassionate toward what is harmful, a hostile mind is established; when a hostile mind is established, there is wrong view.
For one with wrong view, Lohicca, I declare one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.
2. Three Who Deserve Reprimand:
"Lohicca, there are these three teachers in the world who deserve reprimand;
and when one reprimands such teachers, that reprimand is true, factual, righteous, and blameless."
Which three?
Here, Lohicca, a certain teacher has gone forth from the household life into homelessness for a certain purpose, yet he has not attained that goal of the ascetic life.
Without having attained that goal of the ascetic life, he teaches the Dhamma to his disciples:
‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.
Yet his disciples do not wish to hear, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understand, and they proceed contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
He should be exhorted in this way:

“Venerable sir, you have not yet attained that goal of the ascetic life for the sake of which you went forth from the home life into homelessness. Without having attained that goal of the ascetic life, you teach the Dhamma to your disciples, saying:
‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.
Yet your disciples do not wish to hear, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understand, and they proceed contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.”
"Just as one might try to embrace someone who is backing away, or embrace someone with their back turned to you—
even so, I say, is this evil state of greed.
For what can one person do for another?"
This, Lohicca, is the first kind of teacher who is worthy of being reproved in the world;
and when anyone reproves such a teacher, that reproof is true, correct, righteous, and blameless.
Furthermore, Lohicca, there is another kind of teacher here whose purpose for which he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness has not been attained.
Thus, without having attained that goal of the ascetic life, he teaches the Dhamma to his disciples, saying:
“This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.
His disciples listen, lend an ear, apply their minds to understanding, and do not act contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
Thus he should be exhorted in this way:

"Venerable sir, you have not yet attained that goal of the ascetic life for the sake of which you went forth from the home life into homelessness. Without having attained that goal of the ascetic life, you teach the Dhamma to your disciples, saying:
'This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.'"
‘Your disciples listen to you, lend an ear, and apply their minds to understanding, yet they do not act in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction.
Just as if one were to abandon one’s own field and think another’s field should be weeded, so too, I say, is this evil state of greed. For what can one person do for another?
This, Lohicca, is the second teacher who is worthy of being reproved in the world.”
And whoever accuses such a teacher, that accusation is factual, truthful, righteous, and blameless.
Furthermore, Lohicca, here a certain teacher has attained that goal of the ascetic life for which he went forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having attained that goal of the ascetic life, he teaches the Dhamma to his disciples:
‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.
Yet his disciples do not wish to hear, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understand, and they proceed in defiance of the Teacher’s instruction.
He should be exhorted thus:
“Venerable sir, you have attained that goal of the ascetic life for which you went forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having attained that goal of the ascetic life, you teach the Dhamma to your disciples, saying:
‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.’”
‘Your disciples do not wish to listen to you, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understand, and they proceed contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
Just as if one were to cut an old bond and make another new bond, so too, I say, this is an evil state of greed; for what can one person do for another?’”
This, Lohicca, is the third teacher who is worthy of being reproved in the world;
and whoever reproves such a teacher, that reproval is true, factual, righteous, and blameless.
These, Lohicca, are the three teachers who are worthy of being reproved in the world.
“And whoever reproves such teachers as these, that reproval is true, correct, in accordance with the Dhamma, and blameless.
When this was said, the brahmin Lohicca addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“But, Master Gotama, is there any teacher in the world who does not deserve to be criticized?
“There is indeed, Lohicca, a teacher in the world who does not deserve to be criticized.
“But who, Master Gotama, is that teacher in the world who does not deserve to be criticized?”
“Here, Lohicca, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One … [as before] … In this way,
Lohicca, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue … he enters and dwells in the first jhāna.”
Lohicca, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher, that teacher, Lohicca, is one who does not deserve to be reproved in the world.
And whoever reproves such a teacher, that reproval is groundless, untrue, unrighteous, and blameworthy.
…pe…
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna …pe… the third jhāna …pe… the fourth jhāna.
Lohicca, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher,
that teacher, Lohicca, is one who does not deserve to be criticized in the world; and whoever criticizes such a teacher,
that criticism is unfounded, untrue, unrighteous, and blameworthy.
he directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision.
Lohicca, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher, this too—
Lohicca, that teacher who is not worthy of being reproved in the world, and whoever reproves such a teacher—
that reproach is groundless, untrue, unrighteous, and blameworthy. …pe…
"He understands: 'There is nothing further beyond this state of being.

Lohicca, when a disciple attains such a sublime distinction under a teacher, that teacher, Lohicca, is one who does not deserve to be censured in the world; yet whoever censures such a teacher— [That person is blameworthy.]
“The accusation is false, untrue, unrighteous, and blameworthy.
When this was said, the brahmin Lohicca said to the Blessed One:
“Just as if, Master Gotama, a man were to seize by the hair another man who was falling headlong into a pit of hell, pull him out, and set him down on firm ground;”
In this very way, Master Gotama, having pulled me up as I was falling headlong into hell, you have established me on firm ground.
Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...
Or one might show the way, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama.
Therefore, I go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The Lohicca Sutta is finished; it is the twelfth.
